title: Introduction to the Animal Feed Industry

lessons.title: How the animal feed industry works
lessons.html:
What the feed industry does

The animal feed industry turns raw materials such as maize, soya, sunflower oilcake, wheat bran, fishmeal, vitamins and minerals into balanced feeds for animals. In South Africa the biggest users of commercial feed are the poultry industry (broilers and layers), followed by dairy, beef feedlots, pigs, sheep, horses, aquaculture and pet foods. Without good feed, farmers cannot produce affordable chicken, eggs, milk, pork and beef.

The value chain

  1. Grain and oilseed farmers grow maize, soya beans and sunflower.
  2. Grain storage and processors store grain in silos and crush oilseeds to make oilcake.
  3. Ingredient suppliers supply vitamins, minerals, amino acids, additives and premixes.
  4. Feed mills receive, store, grind, mix, pellet and pack feed.
  5. Distributors and co-ops sell bagged feed to smaller farmers.
  6. Livestock producers feed the animals and sell meat, milk and eggs.

Some feed mills are owned by large poultry or pig companies and only make feed for their own farms (integrated mills). Others are commercial mills that sell to many farmers.

Types of feed products

  • Complete feeds – meant to be the whole diet, such as broiler starter or layer mash.
  • Concentrates – mixed with farm-grown grain or roughage, such as a dairy concentrate.
  • Premixes – small amounts of vitamins, minerals and additives added to rations.
  • Licks and blocks – supplements for cattle and sheep on veld.
  • Pet foods – often extruded kibble for dogs and cats.

Feeds come as mash (ground meal), pellets, crumbles or extruded products.

Feed mills in South Africa range from small mills in country towns that make mostly bagged feeds and licks for local farmers, to large automated plants that produce hundreds of thousands of tonnes a year for poultry and pig integrations. Whatever the size, the same basic steps apply: receive, store, grind, mix, pellet and dispatch.

lessons.title: Rules, organisations and your place in the industry
lessons.html:
Laws that control feed

In South Africa farm feeds must be registered and labelled according to the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947. This law aims to make sure that feeds are safe for animals and people and that the label tells the truth about what is in the bag. Feed mills must also follow the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 to protect workers, and environmental rules for dust, noise and waste.

Industry organisations

The Animal Feed Manufacturers Association (AFMA) represents many commercial feed manufacturers. It promotes good manufacturing practice, feed safety and training in the industry. Many mills also follow quality and food safety systems such as ISO standards and HACCP-based feed safety programmes.

Why feed safety matters

What the animal eats ends up in the food we eat. A feed contaminated with mycotoxins, salmonella, the wrong medicine or a foreign object can kill animals, harm people and cost the mill its customers. For example, some additives used in poultry and cattle feed are poisonous to horses, so mixing them into horse feed by mistake can be fatal. This is why mills control cleaning, sequencing of batches and labelling so strictly.

Jobs in a feed mill

RoleMain work
Intake operatorReceives and samples raw materials, moves them to storage
Mill/mixer operatorGrinds, doses and mixes batches
Pellet press operatorConditions and pellets feed
Packer and out-loaderBags, stacks and loads feed
Quality controllerSamples and tests materials and products
Shift supervisorPlans and controls the shift

Every worker is part of the chain. When you follow procedures, record your work and report problems, you protect the animals, the farmers and the mill.

Key points

  • The feed industry turns grain, oilcake and additives into balanced feeds; poultry is the largest user.
  • Products include complete feeds, concentrates, premixes, licks and pet foods.
  • Farm feeds are controlled under Act 36 of 1947 and must be registered and correctly labelled.
  • Feed safety protects animals and people; mistakes such as wrong additives can kill animals.
  • Every mill worker has a role in safe, quality feed.
